name: Floor joist
seoTitle: Floor joist Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Floor joist: work out spacing from the length and the width. A free construction calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: spacing is what the Floor joist calculator works out, and it gets there from the length, the width and the area moment of inertia (I). That makes it useful for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Floor joist calculator work?
sections.html:
The Floor joist calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports spacing in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the nominal joist size, the wood species and the lumber grade); then you type in the length, the width, the area moment of inertia (I) (Joist details) and the area moment of inertia (I) (Joist details).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Floor joist calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Spacing=on-center joist spacing (s) − Actual thickness (w)
Price per floor joist=2 × (50 × cost of floor joists − price per end joist × waste − 100 × price per end joist) ÷ ((waste × rounded up, ((length − Actual thickness (w)) ÷ (spacing + Actual thickness (w))) + waste + 100 × rounded up, ((length − Actual thickness (w)) ÷ (spacing + Actual thickness (w))) + 100) × rounded up, ((-2 × Actual thickness (w) + width) ÷ (free span)))
Actual thickness (w)=12 × area moment of inertia (I) ÷ (Actual height (h) ^ 3)
Total load per unit area=(384 ÷ 5) × modulus of elasticity (E) × area moment of inertia (I) ÷ (deflection limit × (maximum allowable span ^ 3) × on-center joist spacing (s))
Maximum allowable span=(4 ÷ 5) × (5 ^ 2 ÷ 3) × (6) × (modulus of elasticity (E) × area moment of inertia (I) ÷ (deflection limit × total load per unit area × on-center joist spacing (s)))
Deflection limit=maximum allowable span ÷ deflection

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Second moment of area, opening in quartic centimeters
  • Second moment of area, opening in quartic centimeters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Pressure, opening in megapascals

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Floor joist calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the length, the width and the area moment of inertia (I) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Floor joist calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns spacing, derived from the length, the width and the area moment of inertia (I). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Floor joist calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the length, the width and the area moment of inertia (I), which is 16 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter length in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Length opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (5 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Actual thickness (w) = 0 cm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Floor joist calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
